name: Afghanistan
card_headline: Afghanistan is fighting an on-off border war with Pakistan, remains the only country barring girls from secondary school, and saw opium output rise fivefold in 2026
card_summary: The Taliban government, in power since August 2021, is recognised only by Russia. Taliban and Pakistani forces have traded air strikes and border fire since October 2025. The UN says 21.9 million people need aid and 17.4 million face acute hunger. Girls remain barred from secondary school and women from universities. UNODC puts 2026 opium output near 1,500 tons, up from about 300, a count the Taliban Interior Ministry rejects.
card_local: Afghanistan International reported on 19 November that the Taliban heavily publicised leader Hibatullah Akhundzada's visit to Kabul, and KabulNow relayed the UN finding that at least 30 women were arrested in Herat in June. [1][2]
card_international: AP reports that Russia's deputy prime minister led a trade delegation to Kabul on 12 November, and AP, AFP and Reuters report repeated Pakistani and Taliban claims about border fighting that none could verify. [3][4][5]
card_scholar: ACLED finds the Taliban's control of internal security near complete but political violence rising in Badakhshan and Herat, and the UN's 2026 survey counts opium production near 1,500 tons. [6][7]
context_md: The Taliban seized Kabul on 15 August 2021. [8] Girls were excluded from secondary school in March 2022 and women from universities in December 2022. [9] Russia recognised the Taliban government in July 2025 and remains the only country to have done so. [3] Pakistan accuses Kabul of sheltering the Pakistani Taliban (TTP), which the Taliban deny, and fighting between the two states erupted in October 2025 and has recurred since. [10][5] The UN estimates 21.9 million people, about 45 percent of the population, need humanitarian assistance. [11] About 3.7 million Afghans returned from abroad, mostly from Pakistan and Iran, according to the World Bank. [12]

sections.title: One leader in Kandahar, a reported split with the Kabul ministers, and no organised armed challenge
sections.body_md:
BBC reporting, relayed by Dawn in January, described leaked audio of a speech by Taliban leader Hibatullah Akhundzada to a Kandahar seminary about a year earlier. In it he said internal disagreements could eventually bring the movement down. The BBC describes a Kandahar-loyal faction that wants a strictly isolated emirate and a Kabul faction of ministers, militants and scholars that favours engagement, economic development and more education for girls and women. Mullah Baradar is described as the Kabul group's unofficial leader. Spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid called the report unfounded but did not deny that the recording exists. [13] The BBC account also says Akhundzada ordered phone and internet services cut in late September 2025 and that they returned three days later, which insiders read as the Kabul group overriding him. CPJ puts the nationwide blackout at about 48 hours. [13][8]

On 19 November Afghanistan International reported that the Taliban heavily publicised Akhundzada's visit to Kabul as a major event. [1] The same outlet reported on 13 November that the Taliban are expanding tunnels, underground warehouses and defensive facilities in Kandahar and other provinces. That investigation rests partly on one source who has seen some of the tunnels. [14]

Nothing in the sources this draft read points to an organised armed challenge. ACLED's August analysis calls the Taliban's control of internal security near complete, with political violence rising only in Badakhshan (4 recorded events from June to December 2025, 22 from January to July 2026) and Herat (5, then 14). In July the Homeland Soldiers Front briefly seized the Yaftali Sufla district headquarters. The Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP) claimed four attacks in 2026, three of them in Badakhshan and Herat against Taliban members. [6] The UN Secretary-General's May report says armed opposition groups posed no significant challenge and that ISIL-K, the UN's name for ISKP, claimed no major attacks but keeps operational capability. The UN logged 3,687 security incidents from February to April, up 57.7 percent on a year earlier. [11][15]

lenses.local: Afghanistan International reports the publicised Kabul visit and the tunnel construction, both from outside the Taliban's media system. [1][14]
lenses.international: The BBC's leaked-speech report, relayed by Dawn, is the main international account of the Kandahar and Kabul divide. [13]
lenses.scholar: ACLED expects no sustained challenge to Taliban authority in the short to medium term, with localised unrest likely in Takhar, Baghlan, Kunduz and Faryab. [6]

sections.title: A war with Pakistan that never fully ended: strikes, a disputed Kabul toll and failed talks
sections.body_md:
Fighting in October 2025 followed Pakistani airstrikes, including one in Kabul that targeted the TTP's leader. A ceasefire was agreed in Doha on 19 October, and Turkish and Qatari mediators then failed to get a lasting truce at talks in Istanbul on 28 October. Pakistan says the Taliban will not curb the TTP, and the Taliban say they have no control over it. [10] Pakistan struck Nangarhar and Paktika again on 22 February. Pakistan said it killed more than 80 fighters, the Taliban said at least 18 people died and denied the fighter count, and the UN mission said at least 13 civilians were killed. ACLED dates the strikes to 21 February. [16][17] On 26 February the Taliban announced "large-scale offensive operations". A Pakistani government spokesman said 133 Taliban fighters were killed. An Afghan military source claimed 10 Pakistani soldiers dead and 13 outposts captured, which Pakistan denied. [5]

On 16 March a Pakistani air strike hit the Omid Drug Rehabilitation Center in Kabul. The Afghan government says about 400 people died. [18] Human Rights Watch counted at least 143 killed and more than 250 injured, found no evidence of military use and called the attack a possible war crime. Pakistan's information minister said its strikes hit technical support infrastructure and ammunition storage and did not mention the centre. [19] The UN Secretary-General's report says at least 269 died and counts 764 civilian casualties (372 killed, 392 injured) from 26 January to 31 March, mostly from air strikes. [11]

Pakistan struck Kunar, Khost and Paktika on 10 June and said it killed 26 fighters. The Taliban said 13 civilians died, 11 of them children. [20] After an 18 September suicide attack in northwestern Pakistan that killed 31 people, claimed by a TTP-rooted group, clashes resumed in October along the Paktika, Paktia and Kurram frontier. Pakistan declared a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on 11 October. [21][22] The Long War Journal counts bilateral trade down 95 percent in fiscal 2026 and relays a New York Times report, which Pakistan denies, that Pakistani officials met anti-Taliban resistance groups. [23] UNAMA counted more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries from cross-border violence by September, while Pakistan says militants carried out more than 2,800 attacks this year that killed 3,000 people. [4] This draft found no clash reporting later than 29 October.

lenses.local: Dawn reports that UN monitors found Taliban authorities continued their support to the TTP while moving about 2,000 TTP fighters and their families away from the border. [24]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, AP, AFP and Reuters repeat each side's casualty claims and note that neither could be independently checked. [5][4]
lenses.scholar: ACLED recorded the TTP in over 1,000 violent incidents in Pakistan in 2025 and says the Taliban are reluctant to act against it, while Crisis Group, as reported by Dawn, says Pakistan is the country worst hit by the 2021 takeover. [17][25]

sections.title: Fifth year of the bans: 2.4 million girls out of secondary school, women out of UN offices, a new marriage decree
sections.body_md:
UNESCO says about 2.4 million girls are barred from secondary school, 200,000 more than its previous count, and that the number could approach 4 million by 2030. Afghanistan is the only country that bars girls and women from secondary schools and universities. The Taliban reject calls to lift the ban, including from several Muslim-majority governments, and call it an internal matter. [9] The UN Secretary-General's report says Afghan women working for the UN have been barred from UN premises since 7 September 2025 and that Decree No. 12 formalises gender-based discrimination in the legal system. [11]

UNAMA's April to June update records at least 30 women arrested in Herat from 6 to 8 June over alleged improper hijab, and shops and health facilities told not to serve women without a male guardian. No women took part in the public university entrance exams, which drew 120,000 men. A new decree on judicial separation of spouses makes a woman's marriage depend on her guardian's permission. [26] KabulNow reports that a protest in Herat on 9 June was violently dispersed, leaving one boy dead and 17 people detained. ACLED says Taliban forces killed at least two demonstrators. [2][6]

UNAMA documented judicial corporal punishment of at least 137 people (112 men and 25 women) in the quarter and at least 389 arbitrary arrests and 65 incidents of ill-treatment by the vice and virtue ministry. It also records that the Supreme Court stopped announcing floggings publicly from 22 April, though some continued. [26] On 10 April an attack on a Shia shrine in Herat killed 12 civilians by UNAMA's count, and 45 Shia men were detained in Kabul on 18 June for displaying Ashura flags. The Secretary-General's report gives 11 dead for the shrine attack. [26][11]

lenses.local: KabulNow relays UNAMA's findings on the Herat arrests, the 9 June protest and the decree on marriage. [2]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, with AFP and AP, carries UNESCO's count and the Taliban's refusal to lift the ban. [9]
lenses.scholar: UNAMA's quarterly updates are the main systematic record, and the Secretary-General's report states that the restrictions contravene the UN Charter. [26][11]

sections.title: 74 journalists detained since 2021, outlets shut this year, and a 175th place ranking
sections.body_md:
Reporters Without Borders counts 74 journalists arrested and detained since August 2021, for periods from a week to two years. Its November investigation says Directorate 015 of the Taliban's General Directorate of Intelligence monitors media content, summons critical journalists and raids outlets. Detained journalists described beatings, stun-gun use, mock executions and long solitary confinement. RSF has documented more than 20 national directives restricting the press and ranks Afghanistan 175th of 180 countries, with a score of 19.51. [27] Afghanistan International's summary of the same report gives 77 detained and says the Taliban denied arbitrary detentions. [28]

CPJ says Taliban intelligence agents detained TOLOnews presenter Mansoor Niazi on 7 May and political editor Imran Danish two days later, then raided the Kabul office of TOLOnews' parent company on 10 May and seized staff phones. The Taliban gave no public explanation. [29] UNAMA records that two of three journalists arrested in May were freed on 26 May, that Radio Bamyan was closed on 17 May and reopened on 23 June, and that at least seven radio stations in Kandahar and Ghazni could not continue operating. [26] CPJ adds that live political broadcasts have been banned since 2024 with interviews limited to 68 approved analysts, that 14 outlets in Nangarhar lost their licences, and that Tamadon TV was taken off the air in June. It says the Taliban ran about 15 major television and radio stations and other outlets by 2025. [8] RSF also reports leaked intelligence documents, first published by the exiled outlet 8AM Media, that describe a propaganda programme with a projected budget of 70.7 million afghanis and nearly 1,500 social media accounts. [27]

lenses.local: Afghanistan International carried RSF's findings and the Taliban's denial of arbitrary detention. [28]
lenses.international: CPJ and RSF are the main international monitors, and both describe a system run by the intelligence service. [8][27]

sections.title: Growth of about 4 percent, falling income per head, and a collapsed trade link to Pakistan
sections.body_md:
The World Bank estimates real GDP growth of 4.8 percent for 2025 and projects about 4 percent for 2026, with risks from the Middle East conflict. GDP per person fell 5.6 percent because the return of about 3.7 million Afghans outpaced growth, and the population grew about 11 percent in 2025. Inflation averaged 3.6 percent before reaching 7.6 percent in March 2026. [12] Afghanistan International reported on 18 November that the Bank now projects 3 percent growth in fiscal 2026 and a third straight yearly fall in GDP per person. [30]

Trade through the Pakistan corridor fell by more than 90 percent after the border closed in October 2025, according to the UN Secretary-General. [11] Pajhwok, citing the World Bank, says about 60 percent of Afghan trade runs through Iran, and FEWS NET puts the Iran corridor at about 31 percent of imports. The two figures use different bases. FEWS NET also records wheat prices up 17 percent and vegetable oil up 13 percent from October 2025 to February 2026. [31][32] WFP says staple food prices have risen 20 to 30 percent because of trade disruption from the Pakistan conflict and the Middle East crisis. [33] A Taliban deputy health minister said on 15 November that a medicine supply agreement had been signed with Iran. [34]

Foreign business interest is concentrated in Russia and Central Asia. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk arrived on 12 November with more than 70 businessmen, and the Afghan government says bilateral trade more than doubled in the first eight months of 2026 to over $349 million. Deputy Prime Minister Abdul Ghani Baradar invited Russian firms to invest in mining, factories and special economic zones. [3] Al Jazeera lists about $520 million in 2026 trade agreements with Uzbekistan, a Chinese copper contract at Logar dating to 2008 with a declared investment of nearly $3.4 billion, and a stalled TAPI gas pipeline. [35]

lenses.local: Pajhwok, a Kabul outlet working under Taliban rule, relays the World Bank forecast and its warning about dependence on the Iran route. [31]
lenses.international: AP reports Russian trade and investment talks, and Al Jazeera maps the Taliban's economic ties with Uzbekistan, China and Iran. [3][35]
lenses.scholar: The World Bank's May update links falling living standards to returns, declining aid and the Middle East conflict. [12]

sections.title: Opium output rose about fivefold in 2026, and the Taliban reject the count
sections.body_md:
UNODC's 2026 survey, published in November, estimates poppy cultivation at more than 43,000 hectares, up from about 10,000 in 2025, with a range of 32,000 to 61,000. Poppy was grown in 16 of 34 provinces, five more than the year before, and the north-east holds 76 percent of the area, with Badakhshan the main centre. Opium production rose from about 300 tons to just under 1,500 tons, with a range of 800 to 2,400. UNODC reads the figures as a sign that the ban is losing strength, and notes cultivation is still well below levels before the ban. [7] The Taliban Interior Ministry rejected the report, and a Doha Process counter-narcotics working group opened a two-day meeting in Termez, Uzbekistan, in the same week. [28]

Eradication has been a source of unrest. ACLED ties violence in Badakhshan to disputes over mining regulation and poppy eradication. [6] UNAMA records that in May security forces fired on poppy eradication protests in Argo district of Badakhshan, killing two people, one of them a nine-year-old boy. [26] Neither source puts a figure on what farmers earn from the crop, and this draft found no price data for 2026.

lenses.local: Afghanistan International carried the Interior Ministry's rejection of the UNODC estimate. [28]
lenses.scholar: ACLED links the rise in Badakhshan violence to poppy eradication and mining disputes. [6]
lenses.international: UNODC is the only source of the production estimate in this draft, read through its abstract. [7]

sections.title: 21.9 million need aid, the response plan is barely funded, and nearly six million have been expelled from neighbouring countries
sections.body_md:
The UN Secretary-General's May report says about 21.9 million people, 45 percent of the population, need humanitarian assistance and about 17.4 million face acute food insecurity. It counts 4.9 million children and pregnant or breastfeeding women needing treatment for acute malnutrition, about 94,000 people newly displaced since February and flooding in 31 of 34 provinces in March and April. The 2026 humanitarian plan was 14 percent funded, $240.9 million of $1.7 billion. [11] WFP gave a lower hunger figure in August: 14 million acutely hungry, one in three Afghans, with only one in nine of them reached. WFP says 12 provinces have reached critical acute child malnutrition, the highest number recorded, and that it needs $500 million for the next six months. It puts the plan at 26 percent funded. [33] The two hunger counts use different dates and methods, and this draft did not open the underlying IPC analysis.

Returns are the second pressure. The Secretary-General's report counts 548,603 returns from neighbouring countries from January to April 2026 and about 2.9 million in 2025, and raises concern about possible refoulement from Tajikistan. [11] WFP says close to six million Afghans have been expelled from neighbouring countries since September 2023. [33] Dawn, citing UNHCR in February, reported 5.4 million returns from Pakistan and Iran since October 2023, with more than half of returnee families lacking civil documents and over 90 percent living on under $5 a day. [36] VOA quotes a UNHCR statement that Iran deported 492,300 Afghans in 2026, 85 percent of all returns that year. [37]

lenses.local: Dawn reports the UNHCR survey of returnee households. [36]
lenses.international: UN News and WFP put hunger at 14 million and the response plan at 26 percent funded. [33]
lenses.scholar: FEWS NET expected Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes in Faryab, Ghor and Daykundi through April, easing with a near-average wheat harvest. [32]

sections.title: Russia alone recognises the Taliban, while China, the Gulf and others deal with them without it
sections.body_md:
Russia recognised the Taliban government in July 2025 and remains the only state to have done so. [3] Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi claims more than 40 diplomatic missions in Kabul. Al Jazeera reports that China runs an embassy and that Xi Jinping accepted the Taliban ambassador's credentials in January 2024 without formal recognition. Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE keep a presence, the EU mission works from Kabul, and US ties are described as largely limited to security and intelligence. [35] European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen said on 5 November that EU engagement is not recognition and that any change depends on progress on women's rights. [28]

The United States has been the least predictable. President Trump said in September 2025 that he wants Bagram air base back, the Wall Street Journal reported talks on using it for counterterrorism, and Taliban officials rejected a US military return. [38] This draft found no 2026 reporting on Bagram. Afghanistan International reports that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at a G20 foreign ministers' meeting that Washington shares Pakistan's concerns about terrorism from Afghanistan. That is one outlet's summary. [28]

Regional diplomacy runs through Pakistan's quarrel with Kabul. The eighth Moscow Format meeting ended on 5 October without a joint statement, and Russian envoy Zamir Kabulov said the Taliban objected to repeated links between Afghanistan and terrorism. [21] Afghanistan International reports that the Taliban were not part of the Economic Cooperation Organisation foreign ministers' meeting in Islamabad on 15 November. [39] On 15 June the Security Council voted unanimously to extend the UN mission, UNAMA, to 17 June 2027 on a draft by China. [40]

lenses.local: Afghanistan International reports the EU's position and the Taliban's exclusion from the ECO meeting. [28][39]
lenses.international: AP reports the Russian delegation's visit and its recognition-era trade claims. [3]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group, as reported by Dawn, says Islamabad may strike Afghanistan again if militant attacks continue despite the ceasefire. [25]

timeline.text: Girls are excluded from secondary schools; women are barred from universities in December.
Russia becomes the first country to recognise the Taliban government.
Trump says he wants Bagram air base back; Taliban officials reject a US return.
Afghan women working for the UN are barred from UN premises.
Doha ceasefire between Pakistan and the Taliban; Istanbul talks fail on 28 October.
Pakistani air strikes hit Nangarhar and Paktika; the Taliban launch attacks on 26 February.
A Pakistani air strike hits the Omid Drug Rehabilitation Center in Kabul; tolls range from 143 to about 400.
Taliban intelligence detains a TOLOnews presenter and, on 9 May, its political editor; the parent company office is raided on 10 May.
Pakistani strikes in Kunar, Khost and Paktika; the Taliban say 13 civilians died.
The Security Council extends UNAMA to 17 June 2027.
WFP says 14 million Afghans face acute hunger and can reach one in nine.
A suicide attack in northwestern Pakistan kills 31; clashes with the Taliban follow in October.
Pakistan declares a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
RSF publishes its investigation of Taliban intelligence Directorate 015.
Afghanistan International reports the UNODC estimate of nearly 1,500 tons of opium and the Interior Ministry rejection.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Overchuk leads a trade delegation to Kabul.
Afghanistan International reports on the Taliban leader's publicised Kabul visit.

scores.coverage_basis: AP and Al Jazeera, with AFP and Reuters copy, report on the Pakistan fighting and on visits such as Russia's trade delegation, but this draft found that much of the reporting on Taliban internal affairs comes from diaspora outlets such as Afghanistan International and KabulNow [3][5][1][2]. UN, ACLED, CPJ and RSF output is steady, and several outlets inside the country have been closed or raided [26][6][8].

severity.basis: UNAMA counted 764 civilian casualties from 26 January to 31 March, mostly from Pakistani air strikes, and clashes with Pakistan continued into October, while ACLED finds internal control near complete [11][23][6].
The UN counts 21.9 million people in need and 17.4 million facing acute hunger, WFP says it can reach one in nine, and close to six million have been expelled from neighbouring countries [11][33].
Girls are barred from secondary school and women from universities and UN premises, UNAMA documents floggings and arbitrary arrests, and RSF ranks the country 175 of 180 [9][26][27].
Growth of about 4 percent is outpaced by returns, GDP per person is falling, inflation reached 7.6 percent and trade through Pakistan fell by more than 90 percent [12][11].
Cross-border fighting recurred through October, new restrictions came in on marriage and movement, opium output rose about fivefold and aid funding stayed far below the plan [23][26][7][11].

parts.basis: Russia recognises the Taliban and sent 70 businessmen, China runs an embassy and holds the Logar copper contract, and the US raised Bagram in 2025 [3][35][38].
Opium output near 1,500 tons, about $520 million in 2026 Uzbek trade agreements and a stalled TAPI pipeline are the main outward links [7][35].
Pakistan says militants carried out more than 2,800 attacks this year, the UN calls ISIL-K the main regional threat, and Pakistan and the Taliban trade fire [4][24].
UNHCR data reported by Dawn show 5.4 million returns from Pakistan and Iran since October 2023, and WFP counts close to six million expelled [36][33].
UNESCO calls Afghanistan the only country barring girls from secondary school, the EU ties recognition to women's rights, and HRW calls the Kabul strike a possible war crime [9][28][19].

summary: Afghanistan matters beyond its borders through its war with Pakistan, the return flows from Pakistan and Iran, an opium economy and the open question of recognition, while great-power interest is real but mostly commercial and diplomatic [23][36][7][3].
gi.up: A major Pakistani ground offensive, a mass-casualty attack by ISKP or the TTP, a formal recognition by China or the US, or confirmed foreign basing at Bagram.
gi.down: A durable Pakistan and Taliban truce with the border reopened, and a relaxation of the bans that lets the EU and others normalise ties.

gaps: Local sourcing is limited: domestic outlets such as TOLOnews and Pajhwok work under Taliban pressure and were read once or not at all, so most local-language and local reporting here comes from diaspora outlets (Afghanistan International, KabulNow). Several Afghanistan International pages were readable only as summaries.

Pakistan and Taliban casualty figures are each side's claims. No independent count was found for the February fighting, and the toll of the 16 March Kabul strike ranges from 143 (HRW) through 269 (UN) to about 400 (Afghan government).

No clash reporting later than 29 October was found, so the current state of the Pakistan and Taliban front in late November is unknown. The Pakistani view rests on Dawn and Pakistani officials quoted by AP.
The hunger figures differ (17.4 million in the UN Secretary-General's report, 14 million from WFP); the IPC analysis itself was not opened, and the FEWS NET page has no publication date.

Return figures conflict across sources (World Bank about 3.7 million, UN 2.9 million in 2025, WFP close to six million since 2023, a VOA page with internally inconsistent numbers); periods and definitions were not reconciled.
World Bank growth is 4 percent in the May release and 3 percent in an Afghanistan International headline of 18 November; the newer World Bank document was not opened.
The UNODC opium survey was read through an abstract only, and the Taliban rejection comes from one outlet's summary.
The 38th UN Monitoring Team report, the BBC report on the Taliban split and the Crisis Group text were read only through Dawn's coverage.
Bagram and US policy rest on a September 2025 report and one outlet's summary of a Rubio remark; no 2026 reporting on US talks with the Taliban was found.

Thin on minorities (Hazara and Shia communities beyond UNAMA's incident list), on China's mining and security role in 2026, and on the Taliban's own account of events, which was seen only through quoted spokesmen.

UNAMA's shrine attack toll differs between its own update (12 killed) and the Secretary-General's report (11), and the Herat protest toll differs between KabulNow (one boy) and ACLED (at least two demonstrators).

The only podcast and documentary entries are one 2023 FRONTLINE episode, one August 2026 episode of The World and one Al Jazeera film; no recent English-language podcast with Afghan guests was verified.

reporters.name: Will Selber
reporters.bio: Wrote the 12, 19 and 29 October 2026 Long War Journal reports on Taliban and Pakistani border clashes; the 19 October page describes him as a retired US CENTCOM foreign area officer.
reporters.why: His reports log each clash by date and location and flag which casualty claims are unverified.
reporters.label: FDD's Long War Journal

reporters.name: Pearl Pandya
reporters.bio: Wrote ACLED's 27 February 2026 analysis of the TTP and the Afghanistan-Pakistan dispute and its 13 August 2026 report on internal tensions under Taliban rule.
reporters.why: Her reports put event counts behind claims about the TTP, Badakhshan and Herat.
reporters.label: ACLED

reporters.name: Nazanin Mohseni
reporters.bio: Bylined KabulNow's 28 July 2026 report on UNAMA's finding of a worsening human rights situation.
reporters.why: KabulNow summarises UN human rights findings in plain language for an Afghan audience.
reporters.label: KabulNow

reporters.name: Abdulhaq Omeri
reporters.bio: Bylined the 13 November 2026 Afghanistan International investigation into Taliban tunnel and underground warehouse construction.
reporters.why: One of the few published investigations into Taliban military construction.
reporters.label: Afghanistan International

reporters.name: Amin Ahmed
reporters.bio: Bylined Dawn's 14 February 2026 report on UNHCR return figures and its 9 January 2026 report on Crisis Group's Pakistan findings.
reporters.why: His reports carry UN refugee data and think-tank findings from the Pakistani side of the border.
reporters.label: Dawn

reporters.name: Baqir Sajjad Syed
reporters.bio: Bylined Dawn's 13 August 2026 report on the UN Monitoring Team's findings on the TTP, ISIL-K and Al Qaeda.
reporters.why: The report is the most detailed public summary this draft found of the UN monitors on Taliban links to the TTP.
reporters.label: Dawn

reporters.name: Reid Standish
reporters.bio: Bylined RFE/RL's 19 September 2025 report on Trump's Bagram remarks and the Taliban's response.
reporters.why: The report sets out what was claimed about China and Bagram and what is known.
reporters.label: RFE/RL

reporters.name: Waliullah Rahmani
reporters.bio: Quoted in CPJ's 14 August 2026 statement on journalist repression five years after the takeover.
reporters.why: CPJ is the main monitor of journalist detentions and outlet closures in the country.
reporters.label: CPJ

books.title: No Good Men Among the Living: America, the Taliban, and the War through Afghan Eyes
books.author: Anand Gopal
books.why: Follows three Afghans through the US war and argues the US had a route to victory before it helped revive the Taliban.
books.label: Harvard Book Store (Metropolitan Books)

books.title: The American War in Afghanistan: A History
books.author: Carter Malkasian
books.why: Argues the Taliban outlasted American forces because they saw their fight as one for Islam and against occupation.
books.label: Publishers Weekly (Oxford University Press)

books.title: Afghanistan: A Cultural and Political History, Second Edition
books.author: Thomas J. Barfield
books.why: Traces Afghan politics from the 1500s to the Taliban's return and explains the country's tribal and ethnic structure.
books.label: Princeton University Press

podcasts.title: Afghan women's voices under five years of Taliban rule
podcasts.guest: an Afghan women's rights activist who ran Kabul's last shelter for abused women
podcasts.why: The lead segment follows an activist who ran the last women's shelter in Kabul until it closed in December.

podcasts.title: For Women, 'A Very Different Afghanistan'
podcasts.why: Two filmmakers describe the reversal of women's rights soon after the takeover; the episode is dated.

media.creator: Al Jazeera Media Network ("Making Peace" series)
media.why: Follows a woman in Afghanistan who negotiates with the men who limit Afghan women's lives.

factchecks.by: PERSPECTIVE, from Al Jazeera, HRW and the UN Secretary-General
factchecks.evidence: About 400 is the Afghan government's figure. Human Rights Watch reports at least 143 killed and more than 250 injured, mostly patients, and the UN Secretary-General's report says at least 269 died. Pakistan says it struck military installations and called the Afghan claim false.

factchecks.claim: The Taliban's poppy ban has ended opium cultivation in Afghanistan.
factchecks.evidence: UNODC's 2026 survey finds cultivation up from about 10,000 to more than 43,000 hectares and production up from about 300 to just under 1,500 tons, though still well below pre-ban levels. The Taliban Interior Ministry rejected the report.
